chunks.text: This is repo-story: the Claude Code skill and the Python scripts that turned each of these repositories into the audiobook you are hearing. This chapter walks the skill itself. The next two walk the build scripts that make the audio, and the last walks its tests and the provenance behind it all.
The skill is a pipeline of five phases, and the pipeline is the invariant. Survey, then Explore, then Inventory, then Research, then Narrate.
Survey reads the repository's README and its manifest files and its git remote, then presents a short catalog: project name, author, purpose, tech stack, and how much prompt provenance it can find.

Explore launches one explorer agent per repository to catalog every user-visible feature — exact commands, exact paths, exact defaults — and writes a dossier, one markdown file per repo, into a folder named dossiers.
Inventory reads all those dossiers and groups the features into chapters, orientation first, core workflow next, and writes the plan to a file named inventory dot m d.

Research launches, per chapter, a code-researcher agent that re-verifies current behavior and a prompt-researcher agent that traces each feature to the prompt that shaped it, and writes packets into a folder named research.

Narrate writes beats, then sections, then summaries, and finally a file named chapters dot t x t that lists one section filename per line. That file drives the order of the audio you are hearing. The skill exists because of a single prompt.

In the July twenty-first vendoring session, the user re-pasted his own pre-project plan and called it the kernel of the journey. Verbatim, it read: "Create a system for turning a github repo into a podcast. It will explore the content in the repo for: history and core concepts.

The prose generated will generated for a tts engine and will follow a historical arc and also talk about how this repo adds to the historical arc." The same prompt named the smallest version: "A process you can hand to an AI with a github url that will produce a reasonably small number of chapters that I can read online.

A prompt and an audio output." A repo URL in, chaptered audio out — that is the seed. Note the words "historical arc." The skill you are hearing has deliberately reversed that framing, and I will return to how. The skill runs on a deliberate split between two models.

The main session is pinned to Fable, a Claude model used here as the planner, and it does the planning phases: the survey, the inventory, the beats, and the chapter ordering. The execution phases run only through four named agents, each pinned to Opus, another Claude model used here as the executor.

The four are the explorer, the code-researcher, the prompt-researcher, and the narrator. This split is not prose that asks nicely — it is structural. The settings file pins the session with a two-key object: model, fable; effort level, x-high.
That is a paraphrase of the pin, drawn from the decision record and the recaps. Each agent file pins its own model to opus in its frontmatter.

The decision is recorded in the first architecture decision record, numbered zero-zero-zero-one, titled "Fable plans, Opus executes." Its reasoning, quoted from the record: "Fable is the strongest synthesizer but the wrong price for the token-heavy execution phases; Opus is the strongest generally-priced executor." The record also keeps what it rejected — inline "use model X" instructions scattered across roughly six places in the prose, rejected because prose drifts and relies on the orchestrator obeying it every run.

Structural pins were chosen over prose. And the failure mode is loud by design: if Fable is unavailable, sessions in this repo fail at the model pin rather than silently falling back. Each of the four agents is narrowed to its job.
The explorer is told, in its own file, "do not chase lineage or philosophy." The code-researcher re-reads the source and corrects earlier exploration errors silently.

The prompt-researcher traces each feature to its prompts and is told "never blur the labels." And the narrator's tools are deliberately cut to reading and writing — no shell, no search — because its only job is prose. These four were not always these four.

A July tenth recap names the set as explorer, code-researcher, history-researcher, and narrator; the history-researcher, which once ran web searches for historical context, was deleted and replaced by the prompt-researcher. Between planning and narration sits one handoff artifact: the beats.

The project's glossary defines beats as exactly that — the handoff from planning to narration. For each chapter, the main session on Fable writes a beats file: feature order, the must-hit details pointing at the research packets, the prompt citations, and one-clause transitions.
Then a narrator agent on Opus expands those beats into a section. This structure replaced an older rule where Fable narrated small books inline.

The decision record lists that "two-to-four themes, write inline" approach among its rejected options, replaced so the planning context reaches the narration without paying Fable's price for the volume of prose.
The whole pipeline can also run unattended, and that contract lives in a file named AUTORUN dot m d. As the file itself puts it, the plan is the thinking and AUTORUN is the doing.

It takes a GitHub repository URL, finds prompt provenance in known locations, and works inside one folder per run named after the repo — so that when the build scripts default to their output paths, changing into that folder makes every default just work with no override flags.

Its constraints are firm: no SSH commands; do not publish without an explicit ask, because publishing is the user's own git push; do not clobber prior runs; honor the model split with loud failure; and do not pause mid-pipeline — AUTORUN overrides that to present-and-continue.

Now, that reversal of the founding "historical arc." It came in two moves. On July tenth, the user tried to fix perceived fluff with a sentence-level de-fluff pass in an "understated reportage" register across finished sections.

The recap records that it was reviewed and rejected — it made the content drier without fixing the fluff — and fully rolled back, with a note that any future tone work should happen at the beats level, not by pruning words.
The real fix came on July twenty-second, and it changed the methodology rather than the wording. Verbatim, the prompt read: "the story seems long winded, and a bit too fantastical.

I don't so much as want to provide a historical account as I want to provide a walkthrough of the features and the prompts that influenced the features as they currently exist." That single prompt is the largest shaper of the chapter you are hearing.
The skill's description became "produce audio walkthroughs of their features and the prompts that shaped them." The history-researcher agent was deleted and the prompt-researcher put in its place.

The narrate brief grew a paragraph test that bans scenic openings, extended analogies, and historical lineage. That rewrite of the prompts folder is what produced this very section. Those phases all end with text files. Turning text into a voice is the next chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This chapter walks repo-story itself: the Claude Code skill that reads a repository and writes the walkthrough you are hearing. A repo URL goes in, chaptered audio comes out — a shape set by a founding prompt that called it turning a github repo into a podcast.

The skill runs five phases whose order never changes: Survey, Explore, Inventory, Research, Narrate. Survey catalogs the project. Explore writes a dossier of features per repo. Inventory groups features into chapters. Research verifies the code and traces each feature to its prompt.
Narrate writes the sections and summaries, then a chapters file that sets the audio order.

Underneath is a model split, recorded in architecture decision record zero-zero-zero-one: the main session is pinned to Fable for planning, and four named agents — explorer, code-researcher, prompt-researcher, narrator — are pinned to Opus for execution.

The pins are structural so the rule can't drift, and the session fails loudly if Fable is unavailable. Between planning and narration sits the beats file, the handoff artifact. A separate file, AUTORUN.md, is the unattended contract for full runs.
Prompts drove all of it, most visibly a July twenty-second redirect: the user asked for a walkthrough of the features and the prompts that shaped them rather than a historical account.
That prompt deleted the old history-researcher, added the prompt-researcher, and produced the very methodology this chapter follows.

chunks.text: The sections are written. Now build_audio.py gives them a voice. Start with the command. You run build_audio.py, and it finds every section file, orders them, and turns each one into spoken audio. Voice comes from a single reference recording.

Pass the voice flag and it uses that file; leave it off and the script looks in the voices folder, and when exactly one wav sits there, uses it automatically. Two or more, and it stops, prints the names, and tells you to specify one. Zero, and it stops too.

The voice itself is cloned by Chatterbox, the text-to-speech engine this pipeline runs on. It loads onto a CUDA graphics card, which the script requires, reads the reference recording once to prepare the voice, then reuses that for every line it speaks.

Synthesis runs slower than real time, so a full book is a patient job. The final artifact is book dot m4b, tagged with a title and artist you supply, though the album tag is always the same two words: Repo Story. Almost all of this machinery predates prompt exporting in this project.

The chunking, the voice cloning, the encoding arrive in the earliest commits with no prompt to quote. So for this stretch the provenance is commit messages and one recap, and I'll say plainly when a claim rests on those rather than a recorded instruction.
Where I describe what a commit records, that is paraphrase or inference, not a quote. Consider the chunking.

Text-to-speech does not want a whole chapter at once, so the script breaks each section at sentence boundaries — after a period, question mark, or exclamation point — and greedily packs sentences together up to three hundred characters.

That three-hundred limit has no recorded prompt; it has simply been there since the beginning. Then comes a filter with a real reason behind it. After splitting, the code drops any chunk that contains no word characters at all.

Picture a chunk that is nothing but a quotation mark, three dots, another quotation mark. It carries almost no sound. Fed that, Chatterbox can hallucinate — instead of reading the near-empty text, it reads back the transcript of the voice sample it was cloned from. A voice-sample leak.

The fix, from the July third session, is recorded in the commit message and an in-code comment, not a verbatim prompt: drop the word-character-free chunks before synthesis. The comment also flags a consequence you have to respect.

Dropping a chunk shifts the numbering of every chunk after it in that section, so if you change the filter you must clear that section's cached audio before regenerating, or the cache and the text fall out of step. That cache is the next feature.

Synthesis is expensive, so every chunk is saved to disk under a name built from its chapter number and its position — chapter zero one, chunk zero zero zero zero three, and so on. Re-run the script and, for every chunk whose file already exists, it prints cached, skipping, and moves on.

A long run that dies halfway resumes almost where it stopped. And each chunk is written safely: the audio goes to a temporary file first, then gets renamed into place, so a process killed mid-write can never leave a corrupt chunk behind.
Once a chapter's chunks exist, ffmpeg — the media tool this pipeline shells out to — concatenates them into one chapter wav.
Then the assembly step stitches the chapter wavs into the single book dot m4b, writing a chapter marker for each with its start and end time so a player can jump between chapters.

The final encode is A-A-C at one hundred twenty-eight kilobits, with fast start so playback can begin before the whole file downloads. One detail is deliberately fixed: whatever title you pass, the album tag is always Repo Story, hardcoded.

The July second work that set this metadata survives only as an entry in the project's done list, not as a saved prompt. Next, build_m4a.py — and here the format changes for a reason. This is the production format.
The web player consumes one m4a file per chapter, listed in a manifest, not a single book file; that book dot m4b became the standalone, legacy artifact.

The switch traces to the May twenty-second recap, which records the cause as a diagnosis, not a prompt: the deployed player had moved to a per-chapter model, and a restart-chapter bug surfaced because this pipeline was still producing one monolithic file.
So build_m4a.py re-encodes each chapter wav to its own m4a — this time at sixty-four kilobits, twenty-four thousand hertz, mono, lighter than the book file — named chapter, four digits, dot m4a.

Alongside them it writes chapters manifest dot j-son, listing every chapter with its title, duration, and size. The manifest's version is not a fixed label; it is a content hash, the first eight characters of a hash over each chapter's filename, size, and duration.

Change the audio and the version changes, and the player knows to reload. A chapter whose m4a is missing gets a printed warning and is skipped rather than failing the run. There was no prompt for this switch. It was diagnosed in a browser.

Which brings us to the one feature in this chapter with rich, verbatim provenance: the Full and Summary track split. It comes from the July twenty-first session, and it begins with a worry about the reviewer's time.
The prompt reads: I like how this tells a story, and it is enjoyable to listen to, but I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have.

It asks for two buttons beside the transcript label — Full and Summary — so a listener can hear a condensed version and, in the user's words, not have to spend the huge time investment for the arc if they only want the pertinent details. The user gated the work.

A second prompt that same day: don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me. Only after approving a sample did the third prompt land the feature, and its wording set the shape of the whole pipeline. The summary is good.

Incorporate the UI needed to flip between the summary and full text — add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter. The final step of generating a chapter. That phrase is why the summary pass sits right after the full-audio pass in the chapter loop, not off in a separate stage.

In build_audio.py, a summaries folder triggers a second synthesis run per chapter, cached under its own summary prefix and concatenated to a wav whose summary name deliberately keeps it out of the M4B and out of build_m4a's chapter glob — summaries never enter the book file.

In build_m4a.py those summary wavs become their own summary m4a files, and each chapter in the manifest gains a summary block. The version hash even folds the summaries in, so a summary-only change still busts the cache. Audio alone isn't the product.
For the site to play any of this, it needs transcripts and a manifest that ties the words to the sound.

summary_chunks.text: This part of the artifact is the audio engine: two scripts that turn written sections into spoken chapters. The first, build_audio.py, clones a voice from a single reference recording using Chatterbox, the text-to-speech engine, on a graphics card.

It breaks each section into chunks of up to three hundred characters on sentence boundaries, then drops any chunk with no word characters through a speakability filter that stops the model from reading back its own voice sample's transcript.

Every chunk of audio is cached under a chapter-and-index name and written atomically, so an interrupted run resumes instead of restarting. The chapter audio is assembled into a single chaptered book file, with the album tag always fixed to Repo Story.

A second script, build_m4a.py, produces the format the player actually consumes: one smaller audio file per chapter plus a manifest whose version is a content hash, so any change to the audio busts the player's cache.
Most of this engine predates the point where the project began exporting its prompts, so its provenance is commit messages and one recap, not quotes — paraphrase and inference, honestly labeled.

The exception is the Full and Summary track split from the July twenty-first session: a verbatim worry that the reviewer won't spend the time, gated on a sample summary, then a verbatim instruction to add the summary as the final step of generating a chapter — which is exactly where the summary pass sits in the code.

chunks.text: Last chapter turned sections of prose into audio. This chapter turns that audio into a site you can open and play. Start with build_transcripts.py. This script produces the read-along you may be watching right now: it lines the words up with the sound.
It imports the exact same chunking logic the audio builder uses, so a transcript chunk and its audio are always the same slice of text.

For each chapter it re-runs the split into chunks, then walks chunk by chunk, probing the matching WAV file for its duration and recording a start time and an end time rounded to three decimals. The timestamps are chapter-relative: every chapter's first chunk starts at zero.
If a chunk's WAV is missing, it prints a warning and stops that chapter early rather than guessing. The output is a single transcripts.json holding books, chapters, and chunks.

And when a summary text file exists for a chapter, it emits a second, parallel timeline for that chapter, called summary_chunks, with its own timestamps. That summary timeline is here because a prompt asked for it.

The base alignment feature has no verbatim prompt; it comes from an April commit and a later recap. But the summary_chunks addition traces to the same Summary-track request quoted in the last chapter, from the July twenty-first session. And there is a follow-up fix with a verbatim prompt.
From that same session, prompt twenty-three reads: "when summary is selected the time shown in the chapters pane is still the running length of the full length chapter.

this should be updated when summary is selected." So the summary track now carries its own durations all the way through, and the player shows the roughly four-minute summary length, not the full chapter length, once you toggle to Summary. Next, build_site.py.

This is the assembler: it takes the per-chapter audio and a manifest, adds the player, and writes out a standalone static site. Its current mode is driven by a chapters manifest, one entry per chapter.
A detail worth stating plainly: each chapter's id is zero-based, one less than the manifest's chapter number, because that id indexes the player's arrays directly.
The script copies each chapter's audio into the site, skips files that are already identical by size, and removes stale audio that no longer belongs.

Cache-busting uses an eight-character content hash of the content itself, rather than a fixed version string, so the version label changes only when the bytes change. Build_site.py carries two prompt-shaped details worth naming.
The first is a flag called dash dash feedback dash url, which wires in an optional events endpoint and is off by default.

That flag has a scar: a July twenty-first commit had to restore its argument line, because an earlier scrub of private data had dropped the line and every site build then crashed. The July twenty-first research pass caught that, and there is now a test pinning it, which is next chapter's subject.

The second detail is the favicon, and this one is verbatim and iterative. From the July twenty-first session, prompt thirty-one reports "one small bug, no favicon" and a 404 on the icon request. The first fix reused an old icon.

Prompt thirty-two corrected it: "no use the favicon from their site, not my old wbt icon," followed by the Next Chapter project's web address. So the site now links a proper icon, pinned by a test. Next, luinst. The player itself is not written here; it is fetched.
Luinst is a small bash script that shallow-clones landry-ui, a component repository, and copies one component into place.
You call it with a component path and a destination; it clones into a temporary directory, verifies the component exists, then wipes the destination and copies the component in fresh.

It defaults to an HTTPS clone address, a durable consequence of this machine having no SSH git access, recorded in a May recap rather than a standalone prompt. The fetched player directory is gitignored. Next, the one-command builder: build_book.sh.

This wraps the whole Python pipeline so a folder of chapter text files becomes a standalone, emailable player site with no server required. It can scaffold a new book skeleton or build an existing folder.
It strips leading numeric ordering prefixes from filenames, and if that stripping would collide two chapters, it falls back to original names for all of them.

Its cache handling is tiered: any change to the chapter list clears the whole chunk cache, because the indices shift; a change to one chapter's text clears only that chapter's chunks; a changed summary clears only that chapter's summary chunks.

Before doing expensive work it preflights the text-to-speech dependency and auto-fetches the player through luinst if it is missing. It ends by printing, but never running, the command to zip up the site. The purpose of that script is confirmed verbatim.

From the July twenty-first session, prompt five asks whether the build book script can produce something "so i can see this in the player locally for testing." Prompt six is the user insisting on exactly its defining property: "no, no server, a local only build.

a index file i can point my browser at. no running server." And prompt eighteen ties that same standalone build to the publishing workflow. Then two small servers for local preview: serve.py and serve_chunks.py.

Serve.py is a threaded HTTP server that adds byte-range support, answering range requests with a 206 and streaming sixty-four-kilobyte reads. It exists because opening the site from a file path can't seek audio; a browser needs a real HTTP context to scrub and to cache.

Serve_chunks.py is a companion that publishes a live HLS playlist of chunk WAVs over the local network, marked as an event stream with no end tag so a player keeps re-polling as chunks appear, and it guards against half-written files and path traversal.

These are engineering, from April and July commits; no verbatim prompts survive. Finally, where all this publishes. There is exactly one target: the parent next-chapter repository's GitHub Pages site. No cloud hosting, no deploy scripts, and the owner does the push.

The retarget is verbatim, from the July twenty-first vendoring session, prompt sixteen: "let's replay the commits excluding all personal info and unnecessary info you found (we're not using aws for instance).

modify scripts and files as necessary to have it custom tailored to our purposes." So publishing became: copy the per-chapter audio, the manifest, and the transcripts into the parent site's docs folder, and let the owner push. Every one of these scripts has a test suite and a paper trail.
That is the last chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This part of the artifact turns generated audio into a playable, publishable site.

build_transcripts.py produces the read-along: it re-runs the same chunking the audio used, walks the chunk WAV files for their durations, and writes transcripts.json with chapter-relative timestamps, plus a separate summary_chunks timeline for each chapter's short version.

build_site.py assembles the standalone site: it copies per-chapter audio, versions everything by an eight-character content hash for durable cache-busting, prunes stale audio, carries an optional feedback-url flag, and links a favicon.

luinst fetches the player from landry-ui, a separate component repository, over HTTPS by default, into a gitignored player directory. build_book.sh is the one-command builder: a folder of chapter text in, a standalone site out, with transcripts inlined so no server is needed.

Two small servers, serve.py and serve_chunks.py, provide range-capable local preview and a live network playlist of raw chunks. Publishing has one target: the parent next-chapter repository's GitHub Pages folder. No cloud hosting, no deploy scripts; the owner pushes. Prompts drove the sharp edges.

The July twenty-first sessions fixed the summary time display, corrected the favicon in two steps, insisted on a no-server local build, and retargeted publishing away from cloud hosting, all verbatim in the record.

chunks.text: You have heard how repo-story builds an audiobook and how it plays one back. This last chapter is about the proof that the build works and the paper trail that says where this copy came from. Start with a standing rule. Testing here is not optional and it is not an afterthought.

From the July twenty-first session, the prompt is blunt: "you see your directives to test first write code second right?" A later prompt in the same session ties the practice to the written rules: "write it with the prompts and checks we have codified in our rules here." So the tests come first, red before green, and every feature added in the summary-track work of that session shipped with its test in the same commit.
There is no continuous-integration server and no pytest configuration anywhere in the repo. The suites are three self-contained scripts, run by hand.

The first is test build book, spelled build underscore book dot s-h, a bash suite of eighteen numbered checks that exercises the staging and preflight logic of build book. It runs without a GPU and without touching the text-to-speech model, by staging only or by putting a stub Python on the path.
The checks have teeth. No arguments produces a nonzero exit and a usage message; a nonexistent chapters directory is rejected, and so is an empty one.
The happy path asserts real output: chapters sorted, the leading number-dash prefix stripped from each filename, a markdown extension rewritten to text, and the content copied through verbatim.

One check changes a single chapter's text and asserts that only that chapter's chunk cache is cleared while its neighbors survive; another adds a chapter to the list and asserts the whole chunk cache clears so the new ordering takes hold.
A later check confirms that when the broken Python environment fails to import the chatterbook engine, the build stops early with the remedy printed, before any fetch or synthesis.

The final checks cover the summary track end to end: summaries staged beside chapters, a changed summary clearing only its own summary chunks, and build transcripts emitting summary chunks whose first line reads back as "Summary sentence." with a real end timestamp.

The second suite is test build m4a, a Python regression that guards one specific behavior. It generates a silent audio file with ffmpeg, the audio toolkit, then runs build m4a in a temporary directory.

It asserts that the summary WAV becomes a file named chapter zero zero zero one dot summary dot m4a, and that the manifest gains a summary block with a plausible duration. Then it does the thing that matters.

It changes only the summary track, forces a re-encode, and asserts that the manifest's version hash changes. The docstring states the fear in plain words: cache-busting must key on all content, not just the full tracks.

This is the test-first companion to the summary feature from chapter two, pinned so it cannot silently rot. The third suite is test build site, which guards the manifest-mode site build, and it protects two things that both broke in real life.

With no feedback flag given, it asserts the feedback URL does not appear in the page, that the favicon rel-equals-icon link is present, and that the chapter audio is copied. Then it passes a feedback URL and asserts the exact address shows up wired into the page.
The docstring names the sharper regression: a prior vendor scrub once dropped the feedback URL's argument definition while the page generator still read it, and every site build crashed.

The favicon half is the test-first companion to the favicon fix from chapter three, committed red-green in both suites. That vendor scrub is the second half of this chapter, and it is where the paper trail lives. This very copy of repo-story is not the original.

It is a scrubbed, commit-by-commit replay of a private repository, produced by the script vendor-repo-story and vendored into the parent project on July twenty-first. The reason it is a replay and not a single squashed import comes straight from that session.
The prompt reads: "I want to keep as much of the history and files as possible to preserve the cross reference integrity." So each original commit is replayed as its own scrubbed snapshot.
The next instruction set the terms: "let's replay the commits excluding all personal info and unnecessary info you found (we're not using aws for instance).

modify scripts and files as necessary to have it custom tailored to our purposes."

Every replayed commit carries a trailer in a fixed format: Replayed-From, colon, repo-story, at-sign, the original short hash, then in parentheses, "scrubbed vendor replay." The original author date is preserved; the committer date is the vendoring day, so authorship survives while the re-commit stays honest about when it happened.

Excluded from the replay: an Amazon Web Services deploy path the project no longer uses, an undeployed infrastructure blueprint, and personal and machine details, which appear as bracketed placeholders where a value was removed.

The script's verify mode re-scans each replayed commit against a banned-token list, because a scrub that misses a single commit is a leak. The prompts drove one more discipline, the sharpest lesson in the book. Midway through, the author realizes the prompt exports themselves are a leak vector.

The prompt: "this does expose that we need to scan our prompts also as a source of private data leakage. I suggest removing them." The correction was immediate and deliberate: "yes, redact, don't delete.
go ahead." That single exchange is the origin of the whole project's rule that prompt exports are outward-facing content, scrubbed inline rather than dropped.
The prompts you have heard quoted throughout these chapters were themselves cleaned under that policy — family names and infrastructure identifiers redacted inline, the prompts kept whole.
Before the leak concerns were closed, they were checked one at a time, enumerated f-one through f-eight, against the vendored source.

A separate prompt then called for the README banner that declares this copy the live one and the AWS path retired, and another, weighing a reviewer's limited time over convention, is why the vendored copy keeps only its one live architecture decision record rather than a stack of superseded ones.

The replay is not a claim on paper. The live git log carries twenty-three Replayed-From trailers, one per vendored commit, each naming the private-repo hash it descends from. Commits from the vendoring day forward carry no trailer; they are native to this project.
And the chain closes with a person, not a script. The final prompt: "do a final check for personal info on all files in the repo that you will push.

if it all checks out, give me the command to flip it public, and i'll push it after that." The scrub, the replay, the inline redaction, the final sweep — and then a human runs the push. Which closes on a plain fact. This vendored, scrubbed, tested copy is not a museum piece beside the real thing.
It is the live pipeline. It is the code that read a repository, wrote the sections, rendered the audio, and built the player for the walkthrough you have just heard.

summary_chunks.text: This last part is the proof and the paper trail: how repo-story tests itself, and how this copy came to live scrubbed inside its parent project. The tests come first by written rule. From the July twenty-first session: test first, write code second.
Every feature ships with a guard, and the suites are three self-contained scripts run by hand, with no continuous-integration server.

Test build book is a bash suite of eighteen checks over staging and preflight — sorted order, the numeric prefix strip, the markdown-to-text rewrite, per-chapter cache invalidation, and a broken Python environment stopping the build early.

Test build m4a is the summary-track regression: change only the summary and the manifest version hash must change. Test build site guards the favicon link and the feedback-URL argument, the latter because a vendor scrub once dropped the wiring and crashed every build.

The provenance is the heart of it. A script replays the private repo's history commit by commit, each carrying a Replayed-From trailer and its original author date; an Amazon Web Services deploy path and personal details are excluded, redactions left as bracketed placeholders.

Verbatim prompts drive all of it — the scrub-before-public decision, the replay-with-exclusions order, and the rule that prompts get redacted, not deleted. Twenty-three trailers verify in the live git log.
And this scrubbed, tested copy is not a description of the pipeline; it is the pipeline that produced the audio you have been hearing.

chunks.text: Meeting the player. The thing playing this narration to you right now is itself the subject of this book. It is landry-ui, a component library written in plain, build-free JavaScript, and its audiobook player is the component we are walking through.

Four chapters: this one is the player's core — how it lists books, models sound, and moves through a recording. The second is the reading surface, the words on screen. The third is going offline. The fourth is how it plugs into the rest of the system, and the tests that hold it in place.

One honesty note first, said once. Almost everything in this chapter was built early, between April and May, well before this project began exporting the prompts that drove it. So for these features no word-for-word prompt survives.

What survives is the commit message and a session note from early April, both of which paraphrase the work rather than quote the instruction. Where even a commit is silent, it is called inference. I will not dress any of these up as the user's exact words.

Start with what you see first: the library view, drawn by a routine named renderLibrary. It lists each book with a single meta line — the chapter count, a middle dot, the total duration — and a small colored progress dot beside it.

That dot is gray when untouched, blue when a book is in progress, green once it is past ninety-eight percent complete. The heading is configurable: the calling page can pass a title, and if it passes none, the word "audiobook" stands in.

That fallback, and a fix so that automatically resuming your last book no longer overrides the library screen, both landed together in a commit on the second of April; the commit message is the only record of the request. Underneath the library sits the resume system.
As you listen, the player writes your position to your browser's local storage every five seconds, and again when you leave the page, and again each time a chapter ends.

It writes two things: a per-book progress record, keyed by the book's index, holding your book-time and how far through you are; and a pointer to the last book you had open. Reopening the page with no other instruction auto-resumes that last book.

There is a subtle rule here, recorded in the session note as a mistake to avoid: when you return to the library, the code must actively forget the last-book pointer, or the five-second save would quietly set it again and pull you back into the book. Now the heart of it — how the player models sound.

A book is not one giant audio file. It is a set of per-chapter files, one small M4A per chapter, and only one is loaded into the single audio element at a time. This is the pivotal architecture decision of the whole component, made in a commit on the twenty-sixth of April.

Why a single file was abandoned is not preserved in any prompt; a later session recap, looking back, remembers the old model as one file that had swelled to gigabytes — impractical to load and seek — so the player switched to per-chapter files.

Because only one chapter is in memory, the audio element's own clock runs chapter-local, and the player computes a book-wide time on top of it: the chapter's start offset plus the local time. Finding which chapter a given book-time belongs to is a binary search across the chapter starts.
That recap is a downstream witness describing the consequence; the instruction that caused the change is inference. That data model surfaces as the chapter panel down one side of the player.
Each chapter is a row with its title, its duration, a progress fill that tracks only while that chapter is the active one, and a small scrubber handle.

The panel is responsive in an unusual way: it declares itself a container, and when it is squeezed below a hundred and fifty pixels wide, the titles and durations vanish and each row collapses to a short label — "Ch" and the number.

That narrow-label behavior is described in the April session note as a container-query feature, again as a summary of the work, not a quote. Next, the transport bar along the bottom. Minus thirty seconds, previous chapter, play and pause, next chapter, plus thirty seconds, and a speed button.

Skipping preserves whether you were playing or paused. The speed button cycles a fixed list — zero-point-seven-five, one, one-and-a-quarter, one-and-a-half, one-and-three-quarters, and two — starting at normal speed and stepping through on each tap, wrapping around.

Speed is deliberately not remembered between sessions. Above those buttons is the track bar, and it is more careful than it looks. Dragging it uses pointer capture, so once you grab the thin bar your drag keeps working even as your finger or cursor strays off it.

While you drag, the fill and the time readout follow you live, and if your target lands inside the chapter already loaded, the audio seeks in real time; only when you release into a different chapter does it load that chapter's file — because loading on every move would thrash the audio.

Small ticks along the bar mark where each chapter begins. One honest detail: the drag math and those chapter ticks are computed against the full book clock, while the passive progress fill uses the summary-aware clock we will meet in chapter two.
In ordinary playback the two agree; in summary mode they do not perfectly coincide. That is simply what the code does at this revision, narrated by no test.

The two commits behind the bar, both on the sixteenth of July, name the behavior plainly — "drag-to-seek across chapters" and a "hover thumb riding the progress edge" — but they fall just before prompt exporting began, so the wording is the commit's, not the user's.

Last, the address bar itself is a control. Each book has a slug, and opening a book pushes a short hash route so the position is shareable; an empty hash means the library. Moving back and forward in the browser moves the player with it.
That routing arrived whole in a single commit on the sixth of May, and only its subject line records the intent. Sound is half the player. The words on screen are the other half.

summary_chunks.text: Meeting the player, in brief. The subject is landry-ui, a plain-JavaScript component library with no build step, whose audiobook player is playing this narration. This chapter is the player's core. The book runs four chapters: the core, the reading surface, offline, then integration and tests.
The features, by name. The library view lists each book with a chapter-count and duration line and a progress dot — gray, blue, or green by how far you are — under a configurable heading.
The resume system writes your position to the browser's local storage every five seconds and on exit, and auto-reopens your last book.

The per-chapter audio model is the pivotal one: each book is a set of separate chapter files, only one loaded at a time with a chapter-local clock, and a book-wide clock plus binary search sits on top. The chapter panel collapses to short "Ch" labels when squeezed narrow.

Transport gives thirty-second skips, previous and next chapter, play and pause, and a speed button cycling zero-point-seven-five up to two. The track bar uses pointer capture so a drag survives leaving the bar, follows live within the loaded chapter, and loads on release into another.

Hash routing puts a shareable slug in the address bar. One honesty note drives the chapter: all of this predates the project's prompt exports, so every attribution is commit-message or session-note paraphrase, and the per-chapter model's reason is inference.

chunks.text: Chapter two: the reading surface. The first feature is the time-synced transcript. The player renders each chapter as a column of chunks, one span of text per chunk, each carrying a start and an end time.

A loop that runs every animation frame binary-searches those chunks by the current playback time and toggles an active class onto the one chunk whose window contains the moment being spoken, so the highlight walks down the page in step with the voice.
Click any chunk and the player seeks the audio to that chunk's start time and plays; if the chunk belongs to a chapter that isn't loaded yet, it loads that chapter first and starts there.
The transcript data arrives as JSON over the network, often after chapter one has already rendered, so the loader re-renders the current chapter's chunks the moment the data shows up.

No verbatim prompt survives for this machinery — it grew from the original build and a June twenty-eighth fix whose commit reads "fix transcript not loading on initial page load." That's provenance from the commit, not a quoted instruction.

The rule underneath it, logged as a lesson in the session note, is that a transcript's chapter index has to be the sequential position in the audio, not the printed chapter number, or the sync drifts from the first gap onward.

Paired with the highlight is follow mode, the button labeled "follow," and it's on by default. When it's on, the panel auto-scrolls to keep the active chunk parked about a third of the way down the pane as playback advances.

The interesting behavior is how it yields: any manual scroll gesture on the transcript turns follow off — a mouse wheel, a drag near the right edge, a touch move — so a reader reaching ahead isn't fought by the auto-scroll.
It re-arms only on explicit navigation: clicking a chunk, clicking a chapter, scrubbing, or stepping to the previous or next chapter.

This came together in a July sixteenth commit titled "transcript follow — visible toggle, re-arm on navigation, fix scroll math." The commit subject names the three shaping decisions, but this predates the prompt exports, so the user's actual words weren't captured. Commit paraphrase only.
The reading mode button, labeled "read," strips the player down to just the transcript.

It hides the back button, the now-playing header, the chapter list, and the whole bottom control bar, and lets the transcript go full-bleed, edge to edge, with a larger base font and a small play-pause button tucked into the header.
Reading mode has no surviving prompt either, but its commit trail reads like the iteration the prompts would have driven.

First, on July sixteenth, "reading mode — transcript-only view." Then, the same day, "reading mode drops the control bar." Then, July seventeenth, "reading mode full-bleed — max-width none, one-rem gutter." Transcript-only, then also drop the controls, then go edge-to-edge.
Three commits showing the steering even without the words. Next, the text-size stepper: two buttons, "A-minus" and "A-plus," that scale the transcript type.

The scale is geometric — each click multiplies by one-point-two-five, and the exponent runs from minus-two to plus-three, so the smallest is about sixty-four percent of the base and the largest about one-point-nine-five times it. The buttons disable at each end.
And what persists across reloads is the exponent itself, stored as an integer, not the computed scale.

Two commits shaped this: July sixteenth added the stepper, and July seventeenth pinned the exact math with a commit titled, almost literally, "text size equals one-point-two-five to the n, n in minus-two to plus-three." No quoted prompt, but that's the clearest case in the chapter of a commit subject echoing the instruction it implements.

Then, scene-break auto-pause. The source marks scene changes with a divider — asterisks the narration doesn't speak. When playback crosses one of those markers during normal forward play, the audio pauses for two seconds, then resumes on its own, a small breath between scenes.
Seeks and chapter changes re-arm the detector without firing it, so jumping around never triggers a spurious pause.

The hold was originally three seconds; a July sixth change shortened it to two, and that change has its own session recap, which is more useful than the commit because it records why the edit mattered operationally.

Shortening the constant from three thousand to two thousand milliseconds is the same number of characters, invisible to the consuming deploy's size-based change detection, which had to be fixed downstream by content-hashing the player. That durability lesson is the recap's real content.

One verified subtlety in the code: the scene-break scan always reads the full-transcript chunks, even in summary mode, so this is effectively a full-mode feature. Which brings us to the centerpiece of this chapter, and the best-documented feature in the whole player: the Full-Summary toggle.
Two buttons, "Full" and "Summary," sitting right after the Transcript label, and they appear only for books that actually carry a summary track.

Switch to Summary and three things change at once — the audio source swaps to the condensed summary recording, the transcript swaps to the summary chunks, and the entire time model swaps to a second clock.

This feature was built July twenty-first, a session that was prompt-exported, so we have the user's own words. The initial request, verbatim: "I like how this tells a story, and it is enjoyable to listen to, but I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have.

I propose a new feature... add two buttons to the right of the Transcript pane label: Full and Summary." The why is right there in the prompt — the reviewer's time budget. The steering chain is what makes this feature worth dwelling on.

After approving the generated summary, the user asked to wire it in and to "add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter" — an instruction that reached past the player into the generation pipeline.

Then a placement correction, verbatim: "move the full/summary buttons to appear after the word Transcript instead of to the left of the text size controls." The buttons had first shipped in the control cluster; that prompt moved them to sit right after the Transcript label, and a test now guards the placement.
Finally the time-model correction, verbatim: "when summary is selected the time shown in the chapters pane is still the running length of the full length chapter.

this should be updated when summary is selected." That single prompt is the direct cause of the summary clock: the player now computes cumulative summary-based start times and durations for the whole book, and because the two clocks don't map onto each other, switching modes restarts the current chapter from its beginning.
Initial ask, placement fix, time-model fix — the correction arc, in the user's own words. A player this size earns its keep offline too.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter two covers the player's reading surface: the transcript panel and everything that acts on the text while the audio runs.
The time-synced transcript highlights the chunk matching the audio's current position, walking the highlight down the page in step with the voice; clicking any chunk seeks the audio to it.
Follow mode, on by default, auto-scrolls to keep the active chunk parked about a third of the way down the pane — a manual scroll gesture turns it off, and explicit navigation turns it back on.
Reading mode strips the player down to the transcript alone, full-bleed edge to edge, with a mini play button in the header.

The text-size stepper scales the type geometrically, each step one-point-two-five times the last, from about sixty-four percent of the base to nearly double, persisting the exponent. Scene-break auto-pause holds two seconds at the unspoken asterisk dividers, then resumes on its own.
The chapter's centerpiece is the Full-Summary toggle, the best-documented feature in the player.

It appears only for books that carry a summary track, and switching to Summary swaps the audio source, the transcript chunks, and the entire time model at once — a second clock built on condensed durations. Prompts drove this chapter unevenly.
Transcript, follow, reading mode, text-size, and scene-break rest on commit and recap paraphrase, since they predate the prompt exports.
The Full-Summary toggle, built July twenty-first, has verbatim prompts showing a correction arc: the initial request, a placement fix, and the time-model fix creating the summary clock.

chunks.text: Chapter three: taking the book offline. One honesty note up front, and it holds for the whole chapter. Everything here was built in a concentrated burst in early April of twenty twenty-six, months before this project began exporting its prompts.

No verbatim prompt survives for any feature in this chapter. What survives instead is unusually rich for a non-prompt source: a detailed session note from the third of April that records the lessons, plus a dense, self-narrating trail of commits.

So every attribution you hear is a paraphrase drawn from those commits and that note, never a quote of the developer's words. Where the note records a lesson, I will say the note records it. Start with what the listener sees: the download button.

In the library view, each book carries a control that pulls the whole thing down for offline listening. Press it and the button immediately switches to a preparing state, its text changing to "Preparing," its tooltip warning you to keep the page open.
Behind that, a function called downloadForOffline goes to work.

It requests a screen wake lock, if the browser supports one, so the device won't sleep mid-download, and it installs a guard against accidental navigation, so a stray tap on the back button prompts a confirmation instead of silently killing the transfer.

Then it fetches the app shell — the page, the styles, the player script, the manifest, the icons — and after that the chapters, one at a time, in order. As each real fetch lands, the button counts your progress: "Chapter one of twelve," "chapter two of twelve," and on.

For every chapter it stores both the full track and, where one exists, the summary track, because offline listening has to work in either mode. When it finishes, the button settles into a downloaded state with a check mark; if a fetch fails, it flips to a retry state instead.
The important structural detail is that everything downloaded goes into a single audio cache, keyed per file. Each chapter is its own cache entry, stored by its own absolute URL.
Adding a new chapter to a book later never invalidates the ones already saved — the download simply skips anything already cached, silently, with no flash in the UI, and fetches only what's missing.
There's also a lightweight status check that runs when the library renders: it probes the first and last chapter of each book, and if both are present it shows the book as already downloaded.

The code's own comment is honest that this is a heuristic, a fast approximation, not a rigorous check that every byte of every chapter is on disk. Next, the service worker — the file sw.js, the piece that makes offline actually work at fetch time. It keeps two caches, and the split is deliberate.
One is named audiobook-shell, holding the application's own files; the other is named audiobook-audio, holding the chapters.
The reason for two is recorded in the session note as an architecture decision: code updates rebuild the shell cache, but they must never wipe the audio you've already downloaded.

So the shell is precached on install and served network-first — fresh when you're online, cached when you're not — while the audio cache is persistent and served cache-first. Once a chapter is saved, it plays from disk and never touches the network again.
That cache-first audio path is where the central lesson of the chapter lives, and it is about seeking. A cached chapter is stored as a single complete file, a normal two hundred response.

But audio players don't ask for whole files; they ask for byte ranges, so dragging the scrubber jumps straight to a spot. The service worker has to answer those range requests out of a file it holds whole.

A helper called serveRange does it: it reads the cached response as a Blob, parses the requested start and end bytes, slices out exactly those bytes, and returns them as a two-oh-six partial response with the correct content-range headers.
The lesson — enshrined in the commit, in the session note, and in the player's own CLAUDE file under "performance lessons" — is how it slices. It uses Blob dot slice, never arrayBuffer.

Reading the file as an array buffer would pull the entire chapter, seven hundred megabytes and up, into memory on every single seek. Blob dot slice returns a lightweight reference to just the requested bytes. The note frames it bluntly as the difference between twenty-second seeks and instant seeks.

A companion lesson from the same session: cache keys must be absolute URLs. An earlier version keyed entries by relative path and the offline lookups missed; the fix, in a commit dated the fourth of April, was to store and look up every chapter by its full absolute URL.
The shape of the download code is also a record of two dead ends, and the note preserves both. The first was a background-fetch API.

A commit adopted it for offline downloads and a later commit reverted it entirely; the note explains that it proved unreliable — partial downloads, no resume, stale state — so the shipped version is a plain sequential fetch straight into the cache. The second was memory.
On tablets, the early download accumulated the incoming bytes and ran out of memory around four and a half gigabytes. Cloning the response stream didn't help, because the browser buffers both copies.

The note records the fix as a byte-counting stream wrapper that hands bytes to the cache without holding the whole file, and the download button was rewritten several times chasing that crash before it settled. One more piece of the audio cache is a recall mechanism.
On activate, the worker deletes any cache that isn't one of its two current ones, and it also evicts two specifically named legacy keys. One is a leftover from the old single-file architecture.

The other is a chapter that shipped with a bad generation — a leaked voice sample — and had to be purged from listeners' already-downloaded caches. That eviction, in a July commit, is the one moment in this chapter later than April, and its purpose is written plainly in the commit subject.

Finally, install. A web manifest, manifest.webmanifest, is what lets the player install as a standalone app. Its name is "Audiobook Player," its short name "Audiobook," its display mode standalone, so it opens without browser chrome. Its background and theme colors are both a near-black.

It declares two icons, at one hundred ninety-two and five hundred twelve pixels, and both files exist on disk. Installability rests on the served page linking that manifest and registering the service worker, which player.js does on load. That's the listener's side.
Now the developer's: how this player ships into other projects, and how it's tested.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter three is about taking a book offline and installing the player as an app.

One honesty note governs it: everything here was built in an early-April twenty twenty-six burst, before this project exported its prompts, so no verbatim prompt survives — every attribution is a paraphrase of the commit trail and a detailed session note dated the third of April. Four features.

First, the per-book download button, downloadForOffline: one press caches every chapter, guarded by a screen wake lock and a refresh-confirmation prompt, counting "chapter i of total" as it goes, storing both the full and summary tracks, with each chapter kept as its own cache entry keyed by absolute URL, so adding chapters never invalidates saved ones.

Second, the service worker, sw.js, which keeps two named caches — audiobook-shell for the app, served network-first, and audiobook-audio for chapters, served cache-first — split deliberately so a code update never wipes downloaded audio.

Third, offline seeking: a serveRange helper slices a cached whole file into byte-range partial responses using Blob dot slice rather than arrayBuffer, which the note calls the difference between twenty-second and instant seeks; a companion lesson is that cache keys must be absolute URLs.

The chapter also carries two dead ends preserved in the note — an abandoned background-fetch API and tablet out-of-memory crashes — plus a legacy-cache eviction that recalls a bad chapter. Fourth, the manifest that installs the player as a standalone app with its own icons.

chunks.text: Chapter four. Adopting the player, and the tests that keep it honest. The player you have been hearing about is a component, and a component has to be fetched into whatever project wants to use it. That job belongs to a shell script named luinst.
You run it with two arguments: the path of the component you want, and the destination directory to drop it into.
Under the hood it makes a temporary directory, does a shallow one-commit clone of the landry-ui repository into it, and confirms the requested component path actually exists in the clone.

Then it does the blunt thing its callers depend on: it removes the destination directory entirely, recreates it, and copies the component's contents in. A fetch is a replacement, not a merge, so the fetched copy is always exactly what the repository holds, with nothing stale left behind.

The typical call pulls the vanilla player into a project's player directory, and the consuming project gitignores whatever luinst drops there, because the fetch is the source of truth. Which repository, and cloned how?

By default luinst clones over HTTPS from the public landry-ui repository, and that default is recent. It exists because of the July twentieth session, where the whole repository was flipped from private to public. The prompt that opened that work read: "this repo will serve the site.
do an audit on landry-ui to see if it is safe to flip public.

wargame that audit to have as much confidence in the analysis as possible." Once the audit passed, the next instruction was two words: "run the gh flip command yourself." A public repository means consumers no longer need SSH authentication to clone it, so the default clone URL became HTTPS.
A follow-up prompt from the same session handled the paperwork: "use my voice, that is fine. fix luinst https path in docs.

then drop them from the todo in the session recap." The SSH form is still there for anyone who wants it, reachable by setting the LANDRY underscore UI underscore REPO environment variable. Next, the embed contract.

Once luinst has dropped the vanilla player into a project, the host page wires it up with three tags and one call: a stylesheet link to player dot css, a script tag for feedback dot js loaded before player dot js, and then a call to RepoStoryPlayer dot init with an options object.

That object is the contract. It takes a container element, which is required; a books array; an audioBaseUrl that defaults to the string "audio slash"; a transcriptUrl; an optional feedbackUrl; and a title for the library heading. Point those at real data and the player runs.

There is a second variant of the player, written in TypeScript with Tailwind and marked use-client, exported as an AudiobookPlayer component. It is deliberately behind the vanilla one, and that is a recorded decision rather than a captured prompt.

The session note from early April lists the reasoning in the user's own shorthand: vanilla JavaScript over React for the canonical player, more portable, no build step, with React described as feature-complete but not yet optimized like vanilla.

Concretely, the React variant runs on the old single-file audio model, one audio element seeking by chapter start-second offsets, where vanilla loads a separate file per chapter. It has no Full-versus-Summary toggle, no reading mode, no text-size stepper, no offline download.

It carries a couple of things vanilla lacks, like arrow-key seeking of ten seconds, but it is the older, un-migrated cousin, kept working and left behind on purpose. One feature crosses that line in an interesting way: the flag button, the control a listener would tap to report a bad transcription.
In the React variant it is fully rendered, a warning glyph that turns red when flagged and posts a small payload to the feedback endpoint. In the shipped vanilla player it is not.
The wiring is all present: feedback dot js fully defines flag, unflag, and is-flagged, the init call starts the feedback module, and the chunk-flag styling sits in the stylesheet in red.

The payload it would send names the project as repo-story, the type as transcription-error, and carries the book slug, chapter and chunk index, the chunk text, and a timestamp. But player dot js never renders the button and never calls those functions.

Flagging is wired and styled and unreachable, and that too is deliberate. The April session note keeps it as a TODO: feedback flagging UI removed, re-add when the backend is deployed. Two small tools round out the toolkit.
There is serve dot py, a threaded development server whose whole reason to exist is that Python's stock file server does not honor Range requests, and audio seeking needs them.

It parses a byte range, replies with a 206 partial-content status and the correct Content-Range header, and streams the file back in sixty-four-kilobyte chunks. And there is check-m4b, a Python validator with no file extension, a fossil of an older architecture.

It confirms that an M4B's moov atom sits at the front for fast starting, printing the exact ffmpeg fix command if it does not, then checks that the codec is AAC, that chapters are present, and that the duration is positive.

The shipped player consumes per-chapter M4A files, not one big M4B, so check-m4b validates a build path the player no longer takes. It is kept, but it is legacy. Finally, the part that earns trust: the tests.
There are two suites, both Node ES-module scripts driving Playwright, the headless browser-automation library, resolved from a local pinned copy.

One is follow dot test dot m-j-s, contracts A through M, written across the un-exported July sixteenth push alongside the follow-scroll and reading-mode work, so its provenance is the commits, not a captured prompt.

The other is summary dot test dot m-j-s, contracts A through G, and it has a verbatim anchor. The July twenty-first session that built the Full-versus-Summary toggle opened with the user invoking the house rule.
The prompt read: "you see your directives to test first write code second right?" That is why the summary contracts exist as a suite rather than an afterthought.

Those contracts check real behavior: that toggling to Summary loads the summary M-four-A and shows chunks starting with the words "Summary one"; that total time reads twelve seconds; that clicking the third summary chunk moves the clock to about three seconds; that summary mode survives a page reload; and that a book with no summaries hides the toggle entirely.

Both suites run against a synthetic fixture built by gen dot s-h, which uses ffmpeg to generate two silent audio chapters and a fake transcript, including one book with summaries and one without, precisely to exercise that last branch. And that closes the book.
This player, the vanilla one, fetched by luinst into the trilogy site, is the one speaking this sentence to you right now.

summary_chunks.text: Chapter four covers how the player is adopted by other projects, and how the tests prove it before it ships.

The fetch mechanism is a shell script named luinst: given a component path and a destination, it shallow-clones the repository, then removes and recreates the destination and copies the component in. A fetch is a replacement, not a merge.
It defaults to an HTTPS clone, with an environment variable to override to SSH.

That default has verbatim provenance: the July twentieth session flipped the repository public, opening with "do an audit on landry-ui to see if it is safe to flip public," after which consumers no longer needed SSH keys.
The vanilla embed contract is a single RepoStoryPlayer init call taking a container, a books array, an audio base URL, a transcript URL, and a title.
A React variant, the AudiobookPlayer component, is deliberately behind: still on the single-file audio model, missing the Full-versus-Summary toggle, reading mode, and offline.
The transcription-error flag button is wired and styled but unreachable in vanilla, pending the feedback backend; only the React variant renders it.
Two small tools ship alongside: serve dot py, a Range-capable dev server for audio seeking, and check-m4b, a legacy validator for a format the player no longer consumes.

Two Playwright suites, follow dot test and summary dot test, carry contracts A through M and A through G against an ffmpeg-built fixture. The summary suite exists because of a verbatim July twenty-first directive to test first and write code second.

chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository. The site you are listening on right now is itself the feature set — a library of three audiobooks about their own making, served as static files with no backend.
This chapter tours that site: what you see and hear, then the prompts that shaped each piece. Start where the listener starts: the landing page, the file index dot h-t-m-l.

Its browser title reads "Next Chapter — a trilogy about its own making." The page is nearly empty markup — a single app container, the player script, then one inline call that hands the player the entire library as data.

Inlined there is an array of three books: landry-ui, then repo-story, then next-chapter itself. Every book credits the same narrator, Brandon Landry, and every chapter title carries a "Chapter N" prefix.

Across the three books there are sixteen chapters and sixteen matching summary tracks, about four and a half hours of audio in total. That the library holds three books, and in that order, is the product of two scoping prompts.

The kernel is verbatim from the July twentieth foundation session, prompt twenty-eight: "the purpose of this project is to create the github page that is the interface to the audio books that talks about the repositories...
i want there to be the audiobook for the landry ui repository and the repo story repository." That fixed the site as a library of self-narrating books — at first, two.
The third arrived the next day, in the July twenty-first vendored session, prompt twenty-one: "I want to add one more repo to the ones that will appear on the project page, this one: next-chapter.

the history of it itself will point to the history of repo-story and landry-ui which will complete the journey story of all of it and put a bow on it." Two books became three, recorded as decision record nine.

The one-line description under each book comes from the July twenty-first trilogy-built session, prompt twenty-eight: "let's also add a brief, one short sentence that describes each book on the index page." The exact title wording — "a trilogy about its own making" — has no dictating prompt; it follows from that trilogy framing, an inference.

Next, the player itself, which gets its own book, so one paragraph here. It gives you a library view, per-chapter navigation with resume, adjustable playback speed, a time-synced transcript with follow and reading modes, and text-size control.
It is vanilla JavaScript, a global called RepoStoryPlayer, with no build step — the landry-ui audiobook component, vendored rather than rebuilt. That reuse was a live decision.

The foundation session records the hesitation, prompt twenty-eight, verbatim: "i am still conflicted about creating from scratch a reduced functionality user interface as opposed to reusing the landry ui." Prompt thirty-five resolves it: "reuse the landry ui, supersede adr 0002 — the tool is the audio book generator and player." And prompt forty-three locks the framing the whole site exists to show: "the product is the player and generator," the demonstration being their composition.

Now the feature built for the reviewer's clock: the Full and Summary toggle. Each chapter ships two tracks — the full arc, running roughly fifteen to twenty minutes, and a summary running three to four. The toggle sits beside the transcript label and flips between them.

It is the best-documented feature in the repo. Its origin, from the trilogy-built session, prompt eleven, verbatim: "I fear the reviewer won't spend the time on it due to the workload they have. I propose a new feature...

add two buttons to the right of the TRANSCRIPT pane label: Full and Summary." The re-issue adds discipline — "Don't do anything yet except generate the summary and show it to me" — so the summary was reviewed as text before any audio or interface existed.

Prompt fifteen approved it and set the build order: "add the summary text as the final step of generating a chapter." Two corrections followed, both verbatim: prompt sixteen moved the buttons "to appear after the word TRANSCRIPT," and prompt twenty-three caught a bug where the chapter pane "is still the running length of the full length chapter" while summary was selected.

The recap records the fix threading a computed summary clock through the whole time model. Underneath the transcript is one durability detail. The read-along data lives in transcripts dot j-s-o-n, about five hundred thirty-six kilobytes of merged timing text.

The page requests it with a cache key that reads v equals a-six-four-a-a-five-five-nine — the first eight characters of the file's own content hash, verified to match the bytes. Change the content, the key changes; leave it, the browser keeps its copy.

No prompt asks for this; it is the repo's "durable over accurate" rule — key on content, not on modification time — an inference. One feature is present but inert, and honesty requires saying so plainly.

The site ships feedback dot j-s: a flag-a-transcription-error control, styled, with the logic to POST flags to a server. But the published page never passes it a feedback URL, and the site has no backend, so a flagged line is saved to local storage and goes no further.
This is partial by design — the backend was retired in decision eight — and the feature degrades quietly rather than breaking. It is vendored code with no next-chapter prompt behind it.

The site is also installable and works offline, through a service worker in the file s-w dot j-s and a web manifest. It precaches the shell, caches each chapter's audio on first play, and slices cached files into partial byte-range responses so you can seek while offline.
Its cleanup list evicts two stale entries: a legacy single-file book, and one recalled bad-generation chapter — chapter one-zero-seven-three — whose bytes had to be replaced under the same name.

This machinery is vendored from the player, with no next-chapter prompt behind it, an inference — though an earlier war-game of the build plan is what forced the same-origin design that makes it work here at all.
A small thing you see in the browser tab: the favicon, in the file favicon dot p-n-g, is the Next Chapter program mark.

Prompt thirty-one from the trilogy-built session reported the bug — "one small bug, no favicon" — and prompt thirty-two corrected the choice: "no, use the favicon from their site, not my old wbt icon," pointing at nextchapterproject dot org.

It is wired through a registry key so the assembler copies it into place. Last, the trail that lets a reviewer check all of this: the files provenance dot m-d and sources dot m-d. The first, auto-generated, pins the player to an exact landry-ui commit.

The second, hand-written, pins each book's source — and records that this third book is narrated only through commit eight-two-nine-five-c-a-e, because, per decision record nine, a book cannot contain its own generation.

That breadcrumb layer answers a foundation-session prompt, twenty-seven: "what mechanism does this repo provide so that the reviewer has an unambiguous breadcrumb trail to follow."

None of the files in the docs folder are hand-written. A script assembles every one of them. That is the next chapter.

summary_chunks.text: This is next-chapter, the public assembly repository, and the static site you are listening on is the artifact this chapter tours.

The landing page, index dot h-t-m-l, carries the whole library inline: three books — landry-ui, repo-story, and next-chapter — each crediting the narrator Brandon Landry, together sixteen chapters and sixteen summary tracks, about four and a half hours.
That three-book shape came from two prompts: a two-book kernel in the July twentieth foundation session and a trilogy addition the next day.

Inside each book runs the player, the vendored landry-ui vanilla component, giving chapter navigation, resume, playback speed, time-synced transcripts with follow and reading modes, and text sizing — a reuse decided live across three foundation-session prompts.

The Full and Summary toggle is the reviewer's time-budget feature, three-minute summaries against roughly twenty-minute chapters, and the most heavily documented feature in the repo, driven by a prompt chain from origin through two corrections.

Supporting pieces: a transcripts file cache-keyed on its own content hash rather than modification time; a transcription-error feedback flag that is present but inert, saving only to local storage with no backend wired; an installable offline service worker with byte-range slicing and legacy eviction; the Next Chapter favicon fixed by a two-prompt exchange; and provenance documents pinning each book's source commit.
The favicon and toggle carry verbatim prompts; the service worker, feedback, and cache key are vendored and stated as inference.

chunks.text: Chapter two. The player from chapter one plays whatever a registry hands it. This chapter is how the published site, the docs directory, gets built from three separate pipeline runs into one thing the player can load. Start with the registry itself: scripts slash trilogy dot json.

It is a small configuration file, and it is the whole plan for the site in data form. It carries a title — "Next Chapter, a trilogy about its own making" — a favicon key, and a list of three books. Each book entry names a slug, a manifest path, a transcripts path, and a one-line description.

The manifest and transcript paths point into per-book pipeline run folders under repo-story, and those folders are gitignored: the inputs are generated outputs, not committed files. No prompt dictates this file line by line.

It is the place where decisions made elsewhere — which three books, what the site is called, which favicon — get written down as config for the assembler to read. Next, the assembler: scripts slash build dash trilogy dash site.

It reads the registry and, for each of the three books, runs the same sequence. It converts that book's chapters manifest into the player's book structure by calling a function named book from manifest — and here is the design choice worth naming. It does not reimplement that conversion.

It imports book from manifest from build underscore site dot py inside the repo-story tree, the same function the pipeline itself uses to build a single book. One source of truth, derived from rather than copied, so the two can never drift apart.

That reuse is the project's standing "durable over accurate" rule applied: no prompt says reuse this function, the rule says it. Having built each book, the assembler copies that book's audio into docs slash audio slash the slug.

It copies each chapter file and, when a chapter has one, its summary file — but only when the destination is missing or a different size on disk. A size-compare skip, so re-running the build does not recopy unchanged audio.
Then it prunes: any file already in the destination that the new manifest does not expect gets reported as removing stale, and unlinked.

Only after the copy does it prefix every filename with the slug, so a book's first chapter becomes, for example, its slug then slash then chapter underscore zero zero zero one, keeping the three books from colliding in one flat player.
The order matters — the copy uses the plain names to find the source files, and prefixing happens after.

The transcripts from all three books get merged into a single transcripts dot json, and the assembler builds the player's cache-busting URL from the content itself: it takes a sha256 hash of the merged bytes and uses the first eight hex characters as a version query string.
Change the transcript content, the key changes; leave it unchanged, the key holds, and the browser keeps its cache. A content hash, not a timestamp.

Then it copies the player's own files — player dot js, player dot css, the service worker, and the rest — from the player source directory, copies the icons folder if present, and generates index dot html with all three books inlined directly into the player's init call.

Notably this generator writes no feedback URL, which is why, as chapter one noted, the feedback panel on the live site is inert. Now the provenance rule, and this is the sharp one. The player component is a copy of an external UI project, landry dash u i.

When the assembler records where the player came from, it will pin an exact commit only when the player directory is genuinely a checkout of that project — it shells out to git, reads the origin remote and the repository's top-level name, and pins the commit hash only if landry dash u i actually appears there.

Otherwise it writes a plain, unpinned description instead. The in-code comment gives the reason: pinning that repository's HEAD would be, quote, provenance theater. A hash that looks like provenance but points at whatever repo happens to enclose the directory is worse than no hash.
